extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law / political science (general readers seeking an account of American federalism)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository analysis of the constitutional and practical principles governing relations between the national (Federal) government and State governments in the United States, including enforcement, judicial limits, doctrines settled after the Civil War, and criticisms of the federal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe rule for the private citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ascertain whether the Federal law is constitutional {i.e. such as Congress has power to pass). If it is, conform your conduct to it at all hazards. If it is not, disregard it, and obey the law of your State."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges practical difficulty for a private citizen to determine constitutionality but notes little inconvenience in practice because Congress and State legislatures generally keep within their respective spheres; questions between them are seldom such as to disturb an ordinary man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy in conflicts between executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the national officer is acting within his constitutional powers, he is entitled to be obeyed in preference to a State official, and conversely, if the State official is within his powers, and the national officer acting in excess of those which the Federal Constitution confers, the State official is to be obeyed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for resolving direct conflicts of commands between national and State executive officers: obedience goes to the officer acting within constitutional authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of judicial power and choice of tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Every citizen can sue and be sued both in State and Federal courts; in some classes of cases one tribunal is proper, in others the other, while in many it is left to the choice of the parties. A plaintiff in State court may later transfer to Federal court if a point of Federal law arises; suits are constantly transferred from State to Federal courts, but not vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains removability/transfer and choice of forum; no appeal from a State court to a Federal court on pure State law; State judges are not bound to follow the Supreme Court on matters of State law (the Supreme Court decision has only moral weight); Federal courts administering State law should follow the highest State court — though Federal courts sometimes act on their own view of State law (especially in commercial cases), a practice criticized as creating a kind of Federal common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum selection considerations (practical factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs often select Federal courts because Federal judges are more independent and less likely to be influenced by bias; jurors are summoned from a wider area and judges exert more authority in guiding juries. State courts are usually more convenient because there is a court in every county while Federal courts are comparatively few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides practical reasons for choosing State or Federal forum: independence and impartiality versus convenience and locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal enforcement machinery and nationwide reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal authority acts upon citizens directly by means of its own officers (custom-house collectors, excisemen); judgments of Federal courts are carried out by United States marshals dispersed over the country with assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This federal machinery is of utmost importance because it enables the central government to make its laws and commands respected everywhere, irrespective of State loyalties or popularity of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of aid and coercion available to federal officers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a United States marshal or other Federal officer is unable to overcome physical resistance, he may summon all good citizens to assist him (posse comitatus). If insufficient, he must call upon the President, who may order national troops or require the militia of the State to overcome resistance. Inferior Federal officers are not entitled to make requisitions for State force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains stepwise measures for enforcement: citizen assistance, presidential intervention, use of national troops or state militia; stresses limits on inferior officers and parallels to common-law posse comitatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses when Federal authority is opposed (resistance and coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the duly constituted authorities of a State resist the laws and orders of the National government, those who disobey Federal authority on the ground of State commands are insurgents against the Union who must be coerced by its power. The coercion is directed not against the State but against the individuals as combined wrongdoers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains legal and practical consequences of state-level resistance: disobedience is treated as individual insurgency; a State cannot secede or lawfully rebel; coercion relates to punishing individuals (treason power cited) rather than to coercing a State as a legal entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post–Civil War settled doctrines about State power
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the Civil War the following doctrines may be deemed established: No State has a right to declare an act of the Federal government invalid; No State has a right to secede from the Union; The only authority competent to decide finally on the constitutionality of an act of Congress or of the national executive is the Federal judiciary; Any act of a State legislature or State executive conflicting with the Constitution, or with an act of the National government done under the Constitution, is ipso jure void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the core constitutional doctrines cemented by the Civil War and subsequent Supreme Court decisions; notes that individuals who disobey Federal authority on State grounds are insurgents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on federal intervention in State matters (constitutional boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in specified cases (e.g., where State legislation or administration transgresses some provision of the Federal Constitution such as that forbidding ex post facto laws or laws impairing the obligation of contracts), the National government has no right whatever of interfering either with a State as a commonwealth or with the individual citizens thereof, and may be lawfully resisted should it attempt to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides normative boundary: federal non-intervention unless constitutional provisions are violated; gives concrete constitutional examples (ex post facto, impairment of contracts) and real-world illustrations (Slave States, brigandage, local lawlessness) of the kinds of state conduct that federal government nevertheless tolerates unless a constitutional violation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical and practical justification for federal 'laissez aller'
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal independence of States is defended as a merit: local government for local affairs; majority rule and local responsibility mean that States should be left to suffer their own mistakes so that experience will instill responsibility and prompt reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes rhetorical/ethical support from democratic, natural, religious, and statesmanlike perspectives; argues federal intervention risks abuse and clashes with the spirit of the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial limits and non-justiciable political questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any court, State or Federal, may decide on constitutional questions in the first instance; but if the question is a purely political one, it may be incapable of being decided by any court, and in such cases the decision of the political departments (Congress or the President) of the Federal government is necessarily final, though liable to be reversed by a subsequent Congress or President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Reconstruction Acts as illustrations where courts could not resolve certain political questions and political departments' decisions prevailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial invalidity (severability) of State law
rubrics_metrics.description: It may happen that a State law is unconstitutional in part only; in such cases that part only will be invalid, and the rest of the law will be upheld. For instance, a criminal statute might be framed to apply retrospectively as well as prospectively; the retrospective part would be bad but the prospective part good for future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains doctrine of severability with a concrete example and constitutional citation (Const., Art. I, §10, par. 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for Federal courts to create 'Federal common law'
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the theory is that State courts control State law, Federal courts not unfrequently (especially in commercial cases) act upon their own view of State law, and have sometimes been accused of going so far as to create a sort of Federal common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote remark cautioning that Federal courts may deviate from strict deference to State precedents in practice, especially in commercial matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: I. Weakness in the conduct of foreign affairs (federation fault)
rubrics_metrics.description: One frequently charged fault of federations is weakness in the conduct of foreign affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains US experience: early years saw failures in managing foreign relations (e.g., ill-treatment by France and England, drift into War of 1812); when external policy interests only part of the Union, particular States can have strong and possibly unfortunate influence (e.g., immigration of Asiatic labourers).

rubrics_metrics.name: II. Weakness in home government (deficient central authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another charged fault is weakness in home government, i.e., deficient authority over the component States and individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses historical instances where State resistance exposed federal weakness (South Carolina 1832, Kansas troubles of 1855-56); notes Civil War and improved communications have strengthened central enforcement but recalcitrant States may still enjoy advantages for resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: III. Liability to dissolution by secession or rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: Federations are liable to dissolution by the secession or rebellion of States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that State sovereignty and federal system contributed to secession of 1861; though now unlikely due to legal/precedential reasons and the cost of the Civil War, the risk existed and was once grave.

rubrics_metrics.name: IV. Liability to division into groups and factions (State combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federations are liable to division into groups and factions by the formation of separate combinations of the component States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical examples (South Carolina and Gulf States, New England in War of 1812); notes that formal State combinations are now less fashionable and party channels have supplanted State organizations as the vehicle of group action.

rubrics_metrics.name: V. Absence of power to legislate uniformly where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Federations may lack the power of legislating on certain subjects wherein legislation uniform over the whole Union is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies this as a common fault of federations and a practical limitation; the text suggests certain national matters may suffer from piecemeal or non-uniform State treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: VI. Want of uniformity among the States in legislation and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Federations often suffer from want of uniformity among the States in legislation and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of uniformity can impede commerce, development, and the coherent application of law and policy across the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: VII. Trouble, expense, and delay from a double system
rubrics_metrics.description: Federations are charged with trouble, expense, and delay due to the complexity of a double system of legislation and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that duplication and complexity inherent in having both State and Federal systems create practical burdens on governance and citizens.
